readings.title: A shelf of useful tools
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When a drill breaks, buying another one seems a reasonable decision. Buying a drill for one small job is harder to justify, especially in a flat with little storage space. This was the problem that led residents of Cedar Court to open a tool library. A former bicycle store became a place where members could borrow items ranging from sewing machines to garden forks. The project began with donated tools and a small membership fee.

At first, the organizers expected the most expensive equipment to be the most popular. Their records surprised them. Simple items such as ladders and folding tables were borrowed more often than powerful machines. Interviews explained why: these objects occupied considerable space at home but were needed only occasionally. The organizers used this information when deciding what to buy next. They also stopped accepting donations they could not safely inspect or repair.

Borrowing was not entirely free of responsibility. Members received a short demonstration before taking unfamiliar equipment home. They agreed to return items clean and report damage, even if they thought they had caused it. The library charged for deliberate misuse but treated ordinary wear as a normal operating cost. This distinction encouraged honest reporting and helped staff remove faulty equipment before another person borrowed it.

After a year, the library had become a meeting place as well as a storage room. A few experienced members offered practical lessons on Saturday mornings. The organizers welcomed this development but kept the borrowing service as their main priority. They knew that a crowded schedule of events could leave too little time for maintenance. Their aim was not to own every possible tool. It was to make a modest collection dependable and useful to the neighborhood.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

options.B: Occasional access to tools without storing them.
options.C: A new factory for manufacturing drills.
options.D: Permanent storage for every resident's bicycle.

readings.title: Quiet hours at the museum
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
The Northbank Museum used to celebrate busy weekends as evidence of success. Yet staff began receiving letters from visitors who avoided those days. Some found the loud films uncomfortable; others could not follow explanations in crowded rooms. Parents of children sensitive to noise described leaving before reaching the main exhibition. The museum decided to reserve the first hour of one Sunday each month for a quieter visit.

Preparing this hour required more than reducing speaker volume. Staff identified doors that closed noisily and displays with flashing lights. They published a simple route guide with photographs so visitors could anticipate what each room looked like. A small rest area remained available throughout the visit. Tickets cost the same as usual, and visitors could leave and return without explaining their reasons to an employee.

The museum initially asked visitors to complete an online questionnaire afterward. Few responses arrived. A volunteer then offered paper cards with three brief questions near the exit, while keeping the online version available. More people responded, including visitors who preferred not to use a phone during the trip. Several pointed out that the entrance queue was still noisy even when the galleries were calm. Staff moved the waiting line into a covered outdoor area where people had more space.

Attendance during the special hour remained lower than at regular weekend sessions. The director did not regard this as failure, since reduced crowding was part of the purpose. Instead, the museum considered whether people who previously stayed away could complete an enjoyable visit. Feedback suggested that many could. The experiment also encouraged the museum to make its route information clearer for everyone, showing how a focused adjustment can improve a wider public service.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

readings.title: Watching birds on a familiar route
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Each Wednesday before work, Arun walks the same path beside a canal and records the birds he sees. He is one of several hundred volunteers in a local wildlife project. None is expected to be a professional scientist. New participants receive a guide to common species and practice with an experienced observer. They are asked to record uncertainty rather than turn a doubtful sighting into a confident identification.

Following the same route may sound less exciting than exploring a different park every week. For the researchers, however, repetition is valuable. If observers continually move to wherever birds are most numerous, their records cannot easily show whether a particular place is improving or declining. The project therefore asks volunteers to keep roughly the same starting time and walking pace. Weather conditions are recorded too, since a windy morning can make birds harder to hear.

In the second spring, several participants reported fewer small birds near a recently cleared bank. The researchers did not immediately conclude that vegetation removal was the cause. They compared records from other stretches of canal and checked whether observation times had changed. The evidence suggested a local decline, but further work was needed to understand it. Meanwhile, the council agreed to leave some sections of vegetation untouched during the next maintenance period.

Arun says the routine has changed his attention more than his timetable. He now notices seasonal sounds that once blended into background noise. Still, he knows the project depends on accurate records, not just enthusiasm. Volunteers who miss a week mark it as missing rather than entering zero birds. A blank record means no observation was made; a zero means someone looked and found none. That small distinction protects the usefulness of the entire collection.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

readings.title: Lunch portions and useful choices
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
At a factory canteen, kitchen manager Rosa was troubled by the amount of rice left on plates. She first assumed that workers disliked its taste. After speaking to several regular customers, she learned that many enjoyed the food but found the standard portion too large. Some sat at desks all afternoon, while others performed physical tasks and wanted more. A single serving size did not reflect these different needs.

Rosa introduced a smaller initial portion with free additional rice. Staff placed a clear sign beside the counter and invited people to ask for more without joining the main queue again. The price stayed unchanged because the meal still included the same choice of vegetables and a main dish. Rosa explained that the purpose was to reduce unwanted food, not to restrict what anyone ate. This explanation mattered to workers who initially viewed the change as a hidden price increase.

For four weeks, the kitchen weighed the rice left on returned plates. It also recorded the amount cooked and the number of meals served each day. Comparing waste alone would have been misleading if attendance had fallen. In fact, meal numbers were similar, while discarded rice per meal decreased. A few workers requested extra portions, and the second serving point prevented a new queue from forming.

The trial did not solve every source of kitchen waste. Vegetable trimmings and unused ingredients needed separate attention. Nor did Rosa assume the same arrangement would suit a school or a restaurant. The useful lesson was narrower: giving customers an easy choice can work better than guessing what everyone needs. The canteen kept the smaller starting portion, continued offering more, and invited feedback before changing any other part of the meal.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

translation.stem: A shared garden can offer more than fresh vegetables. When neighbors work together, they exchange practical knowledge and become familiar with people they might otherwise never meet. Success, however, depends on clear agreements. Members need to decide who will water the plants, how tools will be stored, and what will happen when someone is away. These arrangements need not be complicated, but they should be understood by everyone. A small garden with reliable care may be more useful than a large project that volunteers cannot maintain. By starting with a manageable area and reviewing their experience after each season, a group can learn gradually and build a space that serves the community for years.
translation.referenceAnswer: 共享菜园带来的不只是新鲜蔬菜。邻居共同劳作时会交流实用知识，并结识原本可能永远不会遇到的人。然而成功取决于明确的约定。成员需要决定谁浇水、怎样存放工具，以及有人不在时如何安排。这些规定不必复杂，但每个人都应理解。得到可靠照料的小菜园可能比志愿者无力维护的大项目更有用。从能够管理的小块区域开始，每个季节结束后总结经验，团队便能逐步学习，建设一个长期服务社区的空间。
translation.explanation: 注意 otherwise 表示否则，who/how/what 并列从句作 decide 的宾语，manageable 表示可管理的。

writing.stem: Write an essay entitled Sharing Useful Things. Explain why people may borrow rarely used items, discuss one responsibility of borrowers, and give an example. Write at least 100 English words.
writing.sampleAnswer:
Many useful objects spend most of their lives in cupboards. A family may need a ladder only twice a year, while a neighbor needs one on a different weekend. Sharing such items can save money and reduce the space required for storage. It can also create opportunities for neighbors to get to know one another.

However, borrowing depends on trust. A borrower should understand how to use an item, return it at the agreed time, and report any damage honestly. For example, our apartment building could keep a simple booking list for a shared folding table. The person who borrows it would clean it before returning it. Clear, practical agreements make sharing easier and help a small service continue over time.
writing.explanation: 围绕节省空间与费用、守时归还和如实报告损坏展开，可用共享折叠桌作具体例子。
